clue.text: Novelist's party number ()

definitions.note: the possessive here stands for 'novelist is'; Simon Raven was an English novelist

parts.note: a rave is a large dance party

explanation.surface: A writer's party piece, as if the novelist had a turn to perform.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Raven wrote the novel sequence Alms for Oblivion. The 's after Novelist stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Raven was a twentieth-century English writer of fiction.

clue.text: Compassion (a modicum) for Pecksniff's pupil's wife

parts.note: ruth is an old word for pity or compassion
a pinch is a tiny amount, a modicum

explanation.surface: A dash of sympathy offered to the spouse of a Dickensian student.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, Tom Pinch's sister Ruth marries John Westlock, once a pupil of the architect Pecksniff.
explanation.definitionFit: In Martin Chuzzlewit this character marries John Westlock, who had studied under Pecksniff.

clue.text: Periodical rage

explanation.surface: A magazine that is all the rage.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a fashion magazine, and to be in it means to be the current craze.

clue.text: An account of Gertrude Stein

parts.note: reads like a biography of Stein, but names a book by her whose title also means simply an account

explanation.surface: A biography of the American modernist writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Gertrude Stein gave a set of lectures published in 1935 under this title; the word itself means an account or telling, so the clue is both a description and a title.
explanation.definitionFit: A telling of a story is an account; Stein's 1935 lectures bear this title.

clue.text: Has German composer been vet? Oh, possibly.

indicators.note: possibly suggests the letters of the preceding words could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about whether a great composer once trained as an animal doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals rearranging BEEN, VET and OH.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer of nine symphonies was born in Bonn, in Germany.

clue.text: Poet's connections

explanation.surface: The relatives or contacts of a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Bridges was Poet Laureate from 1913 to 1930; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Bridges was a Poet Laureate, and spans linking two places are connections.

clue.text: Joy was its daughter, wrote Schiller

definitions.text: Joy was its daughter, wrote Schiller

parts.words: Joy was its daughter, wrote Schiller
parts.note: refers to Schiller's Ode to Joy, which calls joy 'Tochter aus' a paradise of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A literary fact about Schiller's famous ode.
explanation.walkthrough: Schiller's An die Freude, set by Beethoven, opens 'Freude, schoener Goetterfunken, Tochter aus ...': joy is the daughter of the Greek paradise of the blessed.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this is the paradise of the blessed dead, which Schiller names as joy's parent.

clue.text: He figured in early comedy denouement by the seat of his pants

definitions.text: He figured in early comedy denouement by the seat of his pants

parts.words: He figured in early comedy denouement by the seat of his pants
parts.note: points to the servant in Gammer Gurton's Needle, where the lost needle turns up in the seat of his breeches

explanation.surface: A character who played his part in an old comedy's ending by luck.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gammer Gurton's Needle, one of the earliest English comedies, the missing needle is found when it pricks the servant Hodge through the seat of his breeches. 'by the seat of his pants' usually means by improvisation.
explanation.definitionFit: The farm servant of Gammer Gurton's Needle resolves the plot when the needle is found in his breeches.

clue.text: One of Thackeray's colonials

parts.note: refers to Thackeray's novel about two American-born brothers, named after their colony

explanation.surface: A character from a Thackeray novel set in colonial America.
explanation.walkthrough: Thackeray's novel The Virginians follows the Warrington twins from the American colony of Virginia.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's novel follows two brothers from the American colony of Virginia, each a native of that colony.

clue.text: Scandinavian mistresses of spin

parts.note: sounds like Nordic public-relations experts, but means the Norse goddesses who spin the threads of fate

explanation.surface: Nordic women who are expert at media manipulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spin' suggests modern PR, but these are the three Norse fate-goddesses who spin the destinies of men.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norse myth three female figures spin and weave the fate of gods and humans.

clue.text: "Peter Pan save me, me his velly nice friend"

definitions.text: "Peter Pan save me, me his velly nice friend"

parts.words: "Peter Pan save me, me his velly nice friend"
parts.note: a line spoken in Barrie's play by the princess Peter rescues from the pirates

explanation.surface: A quotation from Peter Pan, spoken by a grateful rescued character.
explanation.walkthrough: In Barrie's Peter Pan the princess of the Piccaninny tribe, saved from the pirates, declares her loyalty to Peter in these words.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrie gives this line to the Native American princess whom Peter saves from Hook's pirates.

clue.text: Engraver of the French resistance, with some hesitation

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
er is a sound expressing hesitation

explanation.surface: An engraver who joined the French Resistance, though somewhat reluctantly.
explanation.walkthrough: Albrecht Duerer was the great German Renaissance engraver; 'the French resistance' reads as the wartime movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Albrecht Duerer was a German Renaissance artist famous for his woodcuts and copperplate prints.

clue.text: Holy picture initiates painter into early Tuscan art ()

indicators.note: the initiates of the following words are their first letters, the ones that begin them

explanation.surface: A sacred painting introduces an artist to Tuscan art of the early period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initiates' reads as a verb, but here it is the plural noun: the initial letters of PAINTER INTO EARLY TUSCAN ART. A pieta shows Mary holding the dead Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: A pieta is a devotional image of the Virgin Mary mourning over Christ's body.

clue.text: Abducted prince as courier on Rhode Island (America)

parts.note: a courier is a tour guide
RI is the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island
US is short for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A kidnapped royal travelling as a tour courier in New England.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Cymbeline, the king's sons Guiderius and Arviragus were stolen as infants by Belarius.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cymbeline the king's elder son was stolen in infancy and raised in Wales.

clue.text: Bathing beauties tangled in reeds

indicators.note: tangled means the letters of the words that follow are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: Swimmers caught up in waterside plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tangled' signals rearranging IN REEDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea nymphs of Greek myth, daughters of Nereus, live in the water, so they are fair-faced bathers.

clue.text: Some classic tremors exhibited by writers like Burns and Blake

definitions.text: Some classic tremors exhibited by writers like Burns and Blake

parts.words: Some classic tremors exhibited by writers like Burns and Blake
parts.note: describes the poets who shook classical, Augustan taste, with Burns and Blake as early examples of the movement

explanation.surface: Poets such as Burns and Blake caused shudders among the classically minded.
explanation.walkthrough: The movement is usually set against classicism; Burns and Blake are counted as precursors of it, shaking the classical order.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns and Blake are usually counted among the early poets of the movement that followed eighteenth-century classicism.

clue.text: Chap protects damaged Mir in epic poem

indicators.note: protects means the man is wrapped around the other letters

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: damaged means the letters of Mir are knocked out of order

parts.note: Mir was the Russian space station; the wordplay needs an O beside its letters

explanation.surface: A man shields the ruined Mir space station, in the manner of an epic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' should rearrange four letters into RMIO for 'protects' to put inside MAN, but Mir supplies only three: the O is missing from the clue as printed. Marmion is Walter Scott's verse tale of Flodden.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Scott's long narrative poem of the battle of Flodden bears this title.

clue.text: Version of Circe in rare form of fugue

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters within the word rare
a version of the name Circe is its letters in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A rare musical form retelling the story of the enchantress Circe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Version of' rearranges CIRCE into ICERC, and 'in' puts that inside RARE.
explanation.definitionFit: A ricercare is an elaborate contrapuntal instrumental piece, a forerunner of the fugue.

clue.text: Mackenzie's boreal element of love

parts.note: refers to Compton Mackenzie's novel sequence whose title names a cold blast from the north and love

explanation.surface: The cold side of romance in a Scottish author's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Compton Mackenzie wrote The North Wind of Love; 'boreal element' describes a blast from the north.
explanation.definitionFit: Compton Mackenzie's novel sequence The North Wind of Love names a cold blast from the Arctic, the boreal element.

clue.text: Namesake of Roman fellow, friend of Pistol

parts.note: homo is Latin for man, a fellow to a Roman
Nym is Pistol's crony in Shakespeare's Henry V and The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.surface: Someone who shares a name with a Roman friend of a Shakespearean soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol and Nym are Falstaff's hangers-on in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: A namesake shares a name with another, as words of identical spelling share their form.

clue.text: "I mean by a 'vocabulary' one in which no word can be defined in terms of the others" (Bertrand Russell)

definitions.text: "I mean by a 'vocabulary' one in which no word can be defined in terms of the others" (Bertrand Russell)

parts.words: "I mean by a 'vocabulary' one in which no word can be defined in terms of the others" (Bertrand Russell)
parts.note: a quotation from Russell's Human Knowledge with the adjective before 'vocabulary' left out; the solver supplies it

explanation.surface: A quotation from Bertrand Russell explaining a technical term in logic.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed quotation has dropped the word Russell wrote: he speaks of a smallest possible vocabulary, in which no word can be defined from the others.
explanation.definitionFit: Russell's term is the smallest possible vocabulary, in which no word can be defined from the rest.

clue.text: German books with new content reveal shortlived dramatist

indicators.note: the new letter forms the content held within the German word

parts.note: Buecher is the German for books

explanation.surface: German volumes with fresh material uncover a playwright who died young.
explanation.walkthrough: Georg Buechner, author of Woyzeck and Danton's Death, died aged 23. The umlaut is dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Georg Buechner, who wrote Woyzeck, died at twenty-three, so his life was brief.

clue.text: English travel writer acquires new heart for Australian poet

indicators.note: acquires means the writer's name takes in the letter at its heart

parts.note: Gerald Brenan wrote South from Granada about Spain

explanation.surface: A British travel writer gains fresh courage and turns into an Australian poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'acquires new heart' puts N into the middle of BRENAN. Christopher Brennan was an Australian Symbolist poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Brennan was a Sydney poet of the Symbolist school.

clue.text: Lake girl in lawyer's account

explanation.surface: A girl at a lake features in a solicitor's statement.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaucer's Man of Law's Tale, the lawyer's account in The Canterbury Tales, tells of the patient heroine Custance, or Constance.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the German-Swiss lake called Bodensee, and the heroine of Chaucer's Man of Law's Tale.

clue.text: Browning's smiling boy fell dead beside him ()

definitions.text: Browning's smiling boy fell dead beside him

parts.words: Browning's smiling boy fell dead beside him
parts.note: recalls Browning's Incident of the French Camp, where the young soldier dies beside Napoleon, his commander

explanation.surface: A line from Browning about a dying boy soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem ends 'And his ___ beside, / Smiling the boy fell dead': the missing word is the boy's commander, Napoleon.
explanation.definitionFit: In Browning's poem Napoleon is the boy's leader, the commander at whose side he dies.

clue.text: Lord Jim and Lady Windermere are each one, and each are found in one

definitions.text: Lord Jim and Lady Windermere are each one, and each are found in one

parts.words: Lord Jim and Lady Windermere are each one, and each are found in one
parts.note: each is the name of a book or play, and Lord and Lady are themselves forms of rank-based address

explanation.surface: A riddle about two literary works with aristocrats in their names.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Jim (Conrad) and Lady Windermere's Fan (Wilde) are names of works, and the words Lord and Lady are each an honorific rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Jim and Lady Windermere head literary works by name, and Lord and Lady are each a rank-bearing honorific.

clue.text: Golding leader in moral philosophy

indicators.note: in signals the letters lie inside the words moral philosophy

explanation.surface: Golding taking the lead in moral philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across MORAL PHILOSOPHY. In Lord of the Flies he is the boy elected chief.
explanation.definitionFit: In Golding's Lord of the Flies this boy is elected chief of the stranded children.

clue.text: Browning's autobiographical dawn girl ()

parts.note: points to Elizabeth Barrett Browning's verse novel whose heroine's first name is Latin for dawn

explanation.surface: An early-morning heroine based on Mrs Browning herself.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Aurora Leigh is largely autobiographical; Aurora means dawn, so the clue wants the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Barrett Browning's poet-heroine Aurora carries this surname, and Aurora is the Latin for dawn.

clue.text: Dostoevsky's mature version of Wordsworth's boy? ()

definitions.text: Dostoevsky's mature version of Wordsworth's boy?

parts.words: Dostoevsky's mature version of Wordsworth's boy?
parts.note: Wordsworth wrote The ___ Boy; Dostoevsky's novel has a grown man of the same kind as hero

explanation.surface: Asks whether a Russian novelist's hero is a grown-up Wordsworth character.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's ballad is The Idiot Boy; Dostoevsky's Prince Myshkin, The Idiot, is an adult counterpart.
explanation.definitionFit: Dostoevsky's novel and Wordsworth's ballad both use this word for a simple-minded innocent.

clue.text: He "married on his whiskers, upon which property he had previously subsisted"

definitions.text: He "married on his whiskers, upon which property he had previously subsisted"

parts.words: He "married on his whiskers, upon which property he had previously subsisted"
parts.note: Dickens's description in Nicholas Nickleby of the dressmaker's husband who lives on his looks

explanation.surface: A quotation describing a man who lived and married on his good looks.
explanation.walkthrough: In Nicholas Nickleby the idle Mr Mantalini, husband of Madame Mantalini the dressmaker, is introduced this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens writes this of the dandy husband of the milliner in Nicholas Nickleby.

clue.text: West's compleatly shod angler?

parts.note: Morris West wrote The Shoes of the ___; compleatly glances at Walton's The Compleat Angler

explanation.surface: A fully booted angler from the West Country, Walton-style.
explanation.walkthrough: Morris West's novel The Shoes of the Fisherman is about a pope; 'compleat' recalls Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler.
explanation.definitionFit: One who catches fish with rod and line is an angler; the pope is also styled this, after St Peter.

clue.text: Hoped to make an ancient vestment

indicators.note: to make signals that the letters of hoped are used to build something new

explanation.surface: Someone hoped to sew an old ceremonial robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to make' signals rearranging HOPED.
explanation.definitionFit: An ephod is a sleeveless garment worn by Israelite priests in the Old Testament.
